title: State & Local Taxes
description: A wage tax is one line. Rent, sales tax, and the house can be larger.
wolfLine: The state with the smaller wage tax is not automatically the cheaper life.

flat-tax.definition: A state income tax that uses one rate on the taxable wages, instead of a series of brackets.
flat-tax.example: A flat 3% of $60,000 is $1,800. The next dollar is taxed at that same 3%.

lessons.title: No Wage Tax Is Not No Tax
lessons.summary: A state can skip wages and still tax a purchase or a house.

steps.title: Read the missing tax carefully
steps.body:
Some states do not tax wages. This lesson does not grade a list of them, because a list goes stale. Check the state before a move.

A state with no wage tax can still charge [[sales tax]], [[property tax]], or a tax on investment gains. “No income tax” on a job posting is not “no tax.”

steps.prompt: A state with no wage tax charges no tax of any kind.
steps.explain: Sales tax, property tax, or a tax on gains can still be there.

steps.prompt: A job posting says the state has no wage tax. What do you still price?
choices: Sales tax, property tax, and any tax on gains
Nothing. The posting covered every tax
steps.explain: The posting named one tax. The others can still change the move.

steps.prompt: A state wage tax of $0 versus a state wage tax of $2,000. How much wage tax do you save?
steps.explain: $2,000 − $0 = $2,000. That savings is only the wage tax.

steps.prompt: No wage tax does not mean no ___.

lessons.title: Flat or Graduated
lessons.summary: These rates are an example, not a real state.

steps.title: One rate, or a stack
steps.body:
A [[flat tax]] in this example is **5%** of **$40,000**, which is **$2,000**.

A graduated example taxes the first **$20,000** at **2%**, which is **$400**, and the next **$20,000** at **4%**, which is **$800**. The bill is **$1,200**. Neither pair is a real state’s law. The shape is the lesson.

steps.prompt: What is 5% of $40,000 in the flat example?
What is 2% of the first $20,000 in the graduated example?
What is the graduated example’s total tax?
How much more is the flat example than the graduated example?

lessons.title: A City Can Add Its Own
lessons.summary: The state bill is not always the last bill.

steps.title: On top
steps.body:
A city or county may tax wages too. In this example the city rate is **2%** of **$40,000**, which is **$800**, on top of whatever the state charges.

The lesson is the extra line. The 2% is not a national city rate.

steps.prompt: What is 2% of $40,000?
The state tax in this example is $2,000 and the city tax is $800. What do they add up to?
Where does a city wage tax sit?
choices: On top of the state tax, when the city charges one
Instead of the federal standard deduction
steps.explain: It is an extra income tax. It is not FICA and it is not the federal deduction.

steps.prompt: If the state tax is $2,000, no city can add more.
steps.explain: This example’s city adds $800. Some places have no city tax. The paycheck is where you look.

lessons.title: Property Tax, One Bill
lessons.summary: The rate is local. The bill in front of you is the number.

steps.title: Use the bill
steps.body:
[[Property tax]] is still the local tax on the home. This city’s bill is **$2,400** for the year, which is **$200** a month.

A different city can bill a different amount on a similar house. Do not carry this $2,400 with you as a national rate.

steps.prompt: What is the yearly bill on this page?
What is that $2,400 per month?
Another city bills $1,200 for the year. How much less is that per year?
This $2,400 is the property tax in every city.
steps.explain: It is this bill. The next city has its own.

lessons.title: Sales Tax Is Local Too
lessons.summary: The price on the shelf is not always the price you pay.

steps.title: At the register
steps.body:
[[Sales tax]] is added at purchase. A **$50** item with **6%** sales tax costs **$3** in tax and **$53** in all.

A state that skips a wage tax may still charge this. The 6% is this example’s rate.

steps.prompt: What is 6% sales tax on a $50 item?
What do you pay in all?
The same $50 item in a place with no sales tax costs $50. How much more is the 6% place?
Sales tax is withheld from the paycheck like FICA.
steps.explain: You pay it at the register. It is not a line on the W-2.

lessons.title: Moving Mid-Year
lessons.summary: Two states can mean two returns.

steps.title: This example’s rule
steps.body:
You earned **$30,000** in state A and **$20,000** in state B. In this example, each state taxes only the wages you earned there. State A’s wage tax is **0**. State B’s tax is **5%** of its **$20,000**, which is **$1,000**.

Real states split income in more than one way. The lesson is that a move can create two filings. Check both states.

steps.prompt: What is 5% of the $20,000 earned in state B?
What are the wages in the two states together?
Why might you file two state returns?
choices: You earned wages in both states
The federal standard deduction requires it
FICA is paid to the state
steps.explain: Each state may want a return for the wages earned there. This example’s tax happens to be $1,000, all in state B.

steps.prompt: State A’s $0 wage tax in this example means state B also charges $0.
steps.explain: State B charges $1,000. Each state’s rule is its own.

lessons.title: Two Take-Home Sketches
lessons.summary: Same wages. The state line is the difference.

steps.context: Both sketches use the same **$60,000** of wages and ignore federal tax, sales tax, and rent. Only the state wage tax changes.
steps.prompt: What is state A’s wage tax on $60,000?
What is state B’s wage tax on $60,000?
How much less state wage tax does state A charge?
Looking only at these two state wage taxes, which page leaves more of the wages?
why: State B takes twice as much in this example.
steps.explain: State A takes $1,800. State B takes $3,600.

steps.prompt: The $1,800 gap is your full savings after rent and sales tax.
steps.explain: This pair ignores rent and sales tax. Either one can be larger than the wage-tax gap.

lessons.title: Leo’s Offer
lessons.summary: The wage-tax savings lose to the rent.

story.title: Leo’s two offers
story.body:
Leo is 31 and an electrician. Both offers pay **$60,000**. State A’s wage tax in this example is **$1,800**. State B’s is **$3,600**. State A saves **$1,800** of wage tax.

Rent in state A costs **$400** more a month, which is **$4,800** a year. The tax savings do not cover the rent.

State A costs **$3,000** more after that rent. A missing wage tax, or a smaller one, is not a cheaper life until the rent and the other taxes are on the same page.

steps.prompt: How much wage tax does Leo save in state A?
What is $400 more rent for 12 months?
How much more does state A cost after that rent?
Which offer costs less in this story, once rent is included?
steps.explain: State A’s tax savings are $1,800. Its extra rent is $4,800. State B is $3,000 cheaper here.

steps.prompt: The lower wage tax makes state A the cheaper place to live in this story.
steps.explain: The rent gap is larger than the tax gap. State A costs $3,000 more.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: State & Local Taxes
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: A flat example taxes $30,000 at 4%. What is the tax?
A property tax bill is $1,800. What is the monthly set-aside?
A state with no wage tax cannot charge sales tax.
steps.explain: Sales tax is a different tax. It can still be on the receipt.

steps.prompt: State wage tax is $2,400 and extra rent is $3,600 a year. How much larger is the rent than the tax?
